utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. I apologise for the delay. Before we begin today, there's one thing I would like to deal with in private session. Could we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That said, we'll bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Speaker.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we broke off when we were discussing document D1934.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] so could we call up page 27. I don't know whether the entire transcript has been admitted or only the pages that were displayed earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we admitted it in its entirety, unless I'm mistaken. We'll see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Speaker, please take a look at the penultimate question. A viewer from Pale is asking why Karadzic will not order an attack on Sarajevo as 50.000 Serbs live there and everyone knows it could be done at three days. And then my answer is: "We are trying not to defeat our opponents because we don't want to defeat them, as it is difficult to negotiate with the defeated."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. E-court says only two pages were admitted. If parties could take a look. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what it says here is that we do not want to defeat them and so on and so forth. How does this fit into your own experience, or rather, your own knowledge regarding our general position vis-à-vis our neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is precisely an example of what you advocated as president of Republika Srpska most often, but that was the policy of the political leadership of Republika Srpska then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This last answer here, the question was whether I feel cheated because we released everyone from Manjaca, 5.000 of them, whereas they did not release anyone. And I'm saying that there is a village, an entire village, near Duvno or Livno -- actually, both Livno and Duvno that was turned into a camp. Can you tell the Trial Chamber how we kept our promises and honoured our obligations to release prisoners and how the other side did that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to prisoners, we always insisted on releasing all prisoners on the basis of all for all. And in situations when we talked to the other sides in the presence of the international community or without them, we insisted that prisoners be released. And as a matter of fact, that no one should even be prosecuted, that that should be left for the period after the war, because very often that was the reason why some people were kept in prison. And ultimately it was established that perhaps it only had to do with participation. I very often, on behalf of Republika Srpska, took part in talks that had to do with prisoners. I was helping from the Serb side and from the Muslim side it was Mr. Silajdzic most often, so that the two commissions could resolve some matters of dispute so that prisoners could be released. We insisted then - I as the representative of Republika Srpska - and that was also accepted by Mr. Silajdzic, that prisoners should be released because the very fact that they were kept in prison allowed persons who were not under control to do something bad to the people in prison. I was supported by the entire political leadership, especially yourself, Mr. President, so I could persist in that. But Mr. Silajdzic, in spite of all the efforts he made - and that was obvious - because people at lower levels, especially the chairman of his commission, always disputed that. So let me round this off by saying that we always wanted to have prisoners released as soon as possible everywhere. The example that you gave here, when citizens were objecting and holding this against you, quite simply on the basis of the agreement reached with Mr. Sommaruga, you released all prisoners from prisons and there were many prisoners left on the other side. There was hardly any reciprocity attained, and then citizens criticised you personally and the political leadership for having done that. And you said we have to give a good example and we have to strive for having our people released from prison or from isolation, which is quite similar. This is an example of an entire village that was dealt with in such a bad way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to deal with 73 -- actually, this is new page numbering. Yesterday you were asked about Motika, Oganj, and number 250. Can you tell us briefly who Motika is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I wonder whether parties have checked the pages that have been tendered with respect to this interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, I was -- sent a message to the Registrar because I can't see the notes on e-court. I can only see the document. It doesn't -- mine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have to go to the original. So I would like you to sort it out during the course of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like to suggest that 27 and 28 at least be added if we're not going to admit the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be done at least. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you say briefly why it was that you asked Motika about these weapons? What was Motika then?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milorad Motika at the time was the director of Pretis that dealt with the manufacturing of certain equipment, but also the manufacture of shells, that is to say, combat equipment. Now, why did I ask him that? I tried to explain that yesterday. I was an MP from the area of Sarajevo. Pretis, the company where Mr. Motika worked, was in the area of Sarajevo. It was on the very edge of the front line itself. So I was personally interested in this. My family was there. My father, mother, brother, my family, my neighbours. I knew all the people from that area. Since - how do I put this? - since I was in the top echelons of power of Republika Srpska, people came and spoke to me as friends and asked me to try to help, to call someone so that this area could be protected. Before this conversation - and that was towards the end of the war - there was a major offensive. The civilian population was attacked in the lowest part, Cekrcici, near Visoko, a lot of people were killed because the Muslims wanted in that way, as they said, they wanted to link-up their forces from the city and Visoko, and thus eliminate Serb Sarajevo. Of course, since that is my hometown and -- I called him asking him to help. I asked him for the same thing that my friends and the presidents of the municipalities from there asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, because of overlapping, the interpreters couldn't hear you. But before you repeat your question, what was the exhibit number or 65 ter number where Motika appears? Probably it's one of the intercepts. Mr. Tieger or Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Mr. Tieger will be readier to answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told it's P5653. Yes, please continue. If you could repeat your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Speaker, can you tell us, roughly speaking, how many barrels does Orkan, Oganj, and Plamen have respectively? What is all of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, I'm not very knowledgeable about that. I saw this barrel as I was passing by once. I don't know how many barrels it has. I think that Oganj has one. I don't know. I have to say that I'm not qualified to give a precise answer to that. I heard from them that that is a better thing than an ordinary shell and that's why I asked him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you happen to know about multiple rocket-launchers? Is the size expressed in kilogrammes or calibres?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I'm not knowledgeable about that. I'm sorry. Well, as a layperson I could perhaps say something, but no, I cannot say. I think it's in calibres, if I can say that freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you were asked on page 43839 to 841, you were asked about Orasje, and there was this question put there about to liberate and to gain. And then on page 43846 you said that it was a question of securing the corridor. Can you tell us whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm sorry to interrupt you. I was reading the intercept where Motika appears. Mr. Krajisnik, you just now said that: "... that is my hometown, I called him asking him to help. I asked him for the same thing that my friends and president of the municipalities from there asked me." Could you tell us what it is that they asked for you -- asked you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The presidents of municipalities, there were ten municipalities in Serb Sarajevo -- no, sorry, Sarajevo. One from Ilijas, one from Vogosca, and Rajlovac. These are three municipalities that are closest to Visoko. Very often they would come to see me, as an acquaintance, as a friend, and they asked me, "Can you call someone to come help us?" Then I would either talk to them or try to persuade them that it's not that terrible, or let's say, I tried to pacify them psychologically. Very often the answer I got was: Everything is fine when I'm up here with you, but when we go back, we see that you told us something that was totally unfounded because I didn't really have anything in my hands. It's not that I could do something so I could at least call these people and say: Help these people defend their homes. Make things easier for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I can understand that you tried to pacify them, but in this intercept you asked for some big retaliation, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I explained that. I remember that case very well, that was towards the end of the war. There was this big attack from Visoko, and a lot of casualties on the Serb side. People came and asked me to help them in order to prevent that. Perhaps it's wrong to say "retaliation." It's retaliation towards soldiers, to prevent them from advancing further towards Visoko, which is what they wanted to do and to destroy the population. So my objective was to -- for them to find something so that they would forestall another attack and a pogrom of the population. Perhaps the word "retaliation" was not well chosen, but that was the objective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One of the dialogue -- one of the conversations you had was -- reads like this: "If it's possible, do you have an idea for us to use this opportunity because it's very important to retaliate." So were you suggesting at the time to use an air-bomb at the time for the purpose of retaliation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Well, you see that not even today I don't know what 250 or 350 is. That's what he mentioned, and I just told him that I'm conveying to him what the people on the ground told me about the Oganj and the Plamen. That's all. Later on we spoke in some kind of codes, but I wasn't paying much attention. For example, 250 definitely did not refer to Oganj. It must have been something else, an encryption term for something else. All I was concerned about was whether he was able to help me or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the vicinity of Orasje, were there any Croatian municipalities that, due to the reasons of securing the corridor, we held throughout the war and then eventually returned them to the Croats when the war ended?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately the municipality of Odzak, which is neighbouring to Orasje, we held it the whole time and they -- we returned it immediately. Yesterday I was a bit confused by Mr. Tieger. Namely, you have seen the map and what I was trying to say was that that was not a map -- actually, there were two maps overlapping or superimposed on each other, and I spoke about Orasje in terms of securing the corridor because, from this, let's say, sandwiched area, people were saying that the Croatian forces were constantly attacking. That was the reason. The reason was not to conquer new territories because eventually we returned the territories that we had been holding prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat again the number of pages. It was too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Page 43846, line 15 to 17. "It was simply a question of securing the corridor, and then, again in talks, these things would be resolved politically and not through the military situation on the ground."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So how was the issue of Odzak resolved and settled, politically or militarily?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eventually a political settlement was reached. But I would like to add one thing that you didn't ask me about. There was a permanent danger of passing through the corridor. I myself went that way, and the problem was always if you go by car, people would say: Press your foot on the gas pedal because otherwise you might be shot from the other side or from close proximity. There were even requests to expand the corridor from 1.5 kilometres to, let's say, 3 kilometres for security reasons. Now, as for the ultimate solution, it all depended on the negotiations, and that is what happened at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The day before yesterday, that was page 100 - I'm sorry if I'm wrong - you were asked about the granting of autonomy to the Muslims. How would Muslims would have reacted if we had taken Tuzla and then offered them autonomy within Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you can find a whole series of statements given by people from Tuzla. Tuzla was the most Yugoslav-oriented city with a Muslim majority. For example, had our army occupied Tuzla, I'm convinced that that would be the first area where people would accept autonomy and accept to remain in Republika Srpska just to preserve the town as it had been before, Yugoslav-oriented rather than a fundamentalist one. They would have preferred an autonomy to staying within the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, it was suggested that in a document of General Milovanovic it is said that Karadzic had approved directive 4. The Assembly and the Presidency, where were we physically in November 1992? Were we detached and far away or were we in the town?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency and the Assembly in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, 1992. I cannot remember exactly. I think that we were together for quite some time, and after that we were separated. But I think that at that time we were all together. I cannot remember at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if I had approved the directives that I myself hadn't drafted?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just with a slight reservation I can say that I'm not sure -- that I'm sure that you hadn't approved the directives that you yourselves haven't drafted. Let's say that somebody might have said something on the phone, but in principle, I believe that whatever you signed you had approved; however, what you didn't sign, I don't believe that you approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 93 of -- from day before yesterday, that is, the 19th, it was suggested to you that the term "ciscenje" of the Drina referred to ethnic cleansing. Do you recall what our message to the population was, and do you recall in how many plans we accepted for them to have their own territories and their eastern enclaves along the Drina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for sure that the term "ciscenje" did not mean "ethnic cleansing." That's a military term, and if I remember correctly, this was sanctioned in one of the cases here. Our principle had always been that for a population in a certain area should remain there. There were several statements to that effect. I don't remember when you said that publicly, but I saw documents to that effect. Whoever laid down their arms and was not involved in combat with our army, whoever was loyal and not creating any troubles, they would enjoy the equal rights as the Serbian people. You being a Montenegrin, you often used to say that this is not in the tradition of a Serbian soldier, of a Serbian people, to act unfairly and to commit crimes against other ethnicities who are in the minority and therefore helpless to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown D119 in both versions. This cannot be that number. Well, now we have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is my proclamation dated the 20th of April, 1992. Do you remember us sending this appeal to the Muslims, particularly their civilians?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this proclamation because it was issued only a day or two when I came to Pale. After that we had a platform that you publicly announced which dealt with the same matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 2 it is said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot find the portion that Mr. Karadzic is reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please identify the portions you are reading for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second paragraph, third sentence, fourth line in the Serbian. Let's read the whole paragraph. "The fragmentation of Yugoslavia also led to the transformation of Bosnia-Herzegovina into three units. A number of Muslims and Croats is to live in the Serb Bosnia-Herzegovina and a number of Serbs is to live in the Muslim and Croat Bosnia-Herzegovina. It may be you that is to live in the Muslim or in the Serb Bosnia-Herzegovina. That will depend on a political agreement, which is inevitable. For the time being, you are in the Serb Bosnia-Herzegovina and you are to enjoy the same rights as Serbs do. Many Muslim villages have laid down their arms and are enjoying full protection of the Serb army and Serb state organs. Since at issue is a religious war, we do not force them to fight on our side ..." et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Speaker, can you please tell us how is this consistent with our claims that our vision was to have a pure Serbian republic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This proclamation that you read is consistent with the policy that was being pursued. Let me remind you of the same words that you uttered at the Assembly of 26 July 1992, as well as on other occasions. The policy of the Serbian leadership was not to have a future Serb entity cleansed. On the contrary, always, in all the maps and agreements, it is said that we were in favour of the return of the population that had departed, for everybody to enjoy the equal rights; whereas all those who want to go voluntarily shall have the right to go. That was the point because many Serbs from Sarajevo wanted to leave but were prevented from doing that. We wanted to issue the freedom of movement and to provide the protection for those who were determined to remain behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the platform. Are you referring to the platform of the 22nd of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. I think that took place two days later, therefore it bears this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Speaker, when we mentioned directive 4, are you aware of directive 7? Knowing me as you do, do you believe that I would have consciously approved any directive that would involve violations of international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can claim that Mr. Karadzic would never consciously sign such a directive because, in addition to that, there are a lot of statements and obligations undertaken in which he was advocating completely different things. You yourself and the Serbian side as a whole. I talked with Mr. Miletic about this directive and he himself was surprised - and he drafted it - that this mistake happened. He was in two minds whether that was a mistake or whether that was an intentional deed --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Two matters. First of all, this didn't arise in cross, that's obvious --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it's one of the directives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. But -- so I -- that's why I let it go, but we can see that this is going now in a direction that was clearly -- that is focused in a manner that doesn't implicate the nature of the cross-examination. So the issue of directives generally, okay, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But Miletic saying about this directive 7, if you wish, we'll give you another opportunity to cross-examine this part. Would that be fair, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As I say, I didn't let the general discussion go and this was mentioned anyway at -- he raised it spontaneously in cross, but I realise that it's sometimes necessary to rise in anticipation of where we're headed, which is sometimes why I let leading questions go, like: Are you referring to the platform of ...? But I just wanted to prevent a large-scale effort to venture into areas not raised by cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Krajisnik, during the course of cross-examination you responded to Mr. Tieger's question to the effect that General Miletic himself was surprised by what he himself drafted. But you didn't refer to directive 7. If my memory is correct, I think you mentioned directive 4. But he -- so tell us exactly what Mr. Miletic told you at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since General Miletic was on the same floor as I was and since in my case there are directive -- I don't know if the number was mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, same floor in the Detention Unit ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in the Detention Unit. His cell was adjacent to mine. And since I had been asked about this directive in my trial, but I don't know the number, where it was indicated that the civilians needed to be cleansed or "ocisceni," I was surprised and I reacted by saying that that was a crime and I said the same in my testimony. I asked him the following: I see that you are the author of this directive and you signed it, and I told him how I reacted to it as a witness. He responded by saying that he was surprised too. "I don't know what this is all about, I think it has been misconstrued." Now, I cannot convey to you his reaction verbatim, but I can tell you that he was surprised to see something like that in the directive. And that is what I mentioned this again yesterday or the day before yesterday in response to Mr. Tieger's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. As you know, we have many directives in the -- in this case. What directive were you talking about with Mr. -- with General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The directive where it is said - and we mentioned yesterday - together with the army, the civilian population should leave. That was the phrasing and the language. It was mentioned yesterday, but I honestly don't know the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So did General Miletic admit that he himself drafted directive 4 and directive 7?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about the numbers. I don't know the number of the directive, but the directive mentioned by Mr. Tieger yesterday and the day before yesterday, where he quoted my reaction to the directive, I said that a leading question was put to me. It was later established that it was put to me by Judge Orie, that leading question, and it was in relation to one of the directives. I think -- I don't know myself, but I think it can easily be established which one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll leave it at that. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, yesterday at page -- transcript page - and I'll give you the number in a moment - you were told that our generals visited with President Milosevic. Did you know and did we know, were we informed of the fact that our generals went to visit President Milosevic outside of our knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know. I can only say that I was surprised to see the content of that conversation, if that conversation is indeed credible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was at transcript page --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In that conversation a suggestion is made as if you and I had visited with President Milosevic the day before, allegedly simply so as not to be in the company of generals. In the month of August, around the negotiations surrounding the Dayton Accords, were we in contact with President Milosevic of whatever kind that contact may be?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to set proper dates in that period. What is clear is that for a long period of time, President Milosevic had introduced some sort of an embargo, isolation at any rate, as if sanctions had been imposed against us. I cannot really tell you when this stopped and if that day or two before that date we were there. It's very hard for me to say. I know this was the time when the Contact Group plan was being discussed and when there was a large rift between President Milosevic and our leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did we have more respect for him than he did for us in view of those words that he uttered, referring to us?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do think that we held him in much more esteem than he did us. But I do have my doubts about these words supposedly uttered by President Milosevic, although he was known to be speaking like this and there were occasions when we simply weren't able to accept suggestions coming from him. It is probable that Mr. Mladic added or emphasised these words since he was also in -- on poor terms with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up 30861, a 65 ter document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were our associates aware of our views with regard to the possible capture of Sarajevo or territories not belonging to us? Was this a matter of general knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe that they were aware of it, especially where Sarajevo was concerned. Every president of municipality and citizens in general knew that we did not want to seize Sarajevo. You can look at various reports which even state that foreign officers wondered why the Bosnian Serbs did not go on and capture Sarajevo with their army.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think this is the proper document. Can we have 30861, that's what I was asking for, 30861. Yes, that's the 27th of July. This is a conversation between Momcilo Mandic and one David. Can we look at page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're looking at the bottom half. They're asking about how this -- how the area can be reached. There is a route via Dobrinja, and lastly it says: "Those of our lot wanted to cleanse or mop-up Dobrinja, however, Karadzic would not let them go ahead ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, both versions -- no, sorry. [In English] No, no, this is number one. English may stay. [Interpretation] Right. Perhaps we should have the next page in English. Mandic said that those from Krajina offered to deploy two brigades to ociste, cleanse or mop-up, Sarajevo. However, Radovan would not let them go ahead with that. So can we have the next page again. The English version is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The third line: "They broke through the corridor and want to come to Sarajevo to ociste, mop-up or cleanse it, all the way down there to Herzegovina. However, Krajisnik does not let them ..." and what is missing here is Radovan as well, because was this not your position as well as mine when it came to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the two interlocutors here said is entirely accurate. I don't know, well, about the mention of names here; however, it was your position and that of the entire leadership not to press against Sarajevo militarily because that would result in great casualties and would be detrimental for Republika Srpska, because Sarajevo was a majority Muslim city and we wanted only areas of Sarajevo -- those that were ethnically populated by the Serbs to remain under Serb control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives MFI D4058, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked about the party meeting and the Assembly session which took place on the 21st of December, whereas the party meeting took place on the 19th or the 20th. Though you were not occupied with the dealings of the party, do you know what the reason was for this meeting to be - and I mean the party meeting - to be scheduled as early as it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe that's a misstatement. I think the witness himself said the meeting took place on the 20th. I don't know why -- well, I know why Dr. Karadzic is engaged in this continuing effort, but the witness -- this is a mis-characterisation of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question remains. Do you know why the party meeting was scheduled as it was prior to the Assembly meeting without you being informed of it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alarming news came in of the Muslim side wanting to achieve the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina as soon as possible and contrary to the will of the Serbian people. That's why an urgent meeting was called which was followed by activities, and the subsequent developments showed that our apprehension was justified. It was followed by the plebiscite decision and other very important decisions. Let me just make a remark there. I said that the club of deputies meeting took place on the 20th November. I do not remember if there was a meeting the day before or not. I cannot recall. At any rate, before the Assembly session on the 20th there was a meeting of the club of deputies with other activists coming in from the field.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 32042, a 65 ter document shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document, can you tell the Chamber who is Dr. Dragan Djokanovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Dragan Djokanovic is the president of a small political party called the Party of the Federalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is an intercept, I'm not sure if it's been translated, where Dr. Djokanovic telephoned me and said they are calling on the republics to declare independence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do we not have English version?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: There should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are relying on Mr. Reid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Meanwhile I can read this out for you. Mr. Djokanovic telephoned me in the capacity of the leader of another political party and said that the European community was calling on the other republics to declare independence. The discussion, or rather, this conversation took place on the 17th of December and that they should send the appropriate documents to the European community by the 23rd so that the European community could recognise them by the 15th of January.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the bottom part of the document. Please, can we scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree with me that Mr. Djokanovic suggested that major Bosnia-Herzegovina party should meet in Sarajevo, and he says we can organise a meeting at Holiday Inn and put up strong resistance to this call for the declaration of --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we turn to the next page. [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm not sure we're hearing translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The declaration of independence, so I say: Very well, fine. And then Djokanovic says: What do you think? I wanted to do this with you ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic says: I wanted to do this with you, and I believe that this had to be done as urgently as possible and it should be done as soon as possible in view of the cold weather, et cetera. And further down he says: For the day after tomorrow at 12.00, that's what I say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page. [In English] Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the middle of the page it reads: Well, they said that they would recognise this, but it would come into full effect after the 15th of January. Does the fact that this meeting was called by a different party account for the fact that you were not invited to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular example, as do others, shows that party activities ran alongside and independently of the Assembly activities. So I wasn't aware of what was going on here with a different party that shared the same concern of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D4059, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to what you know of this, was this meeting in fact held at Holiday Inn and what do you know of it if so?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The multi-party meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The SDS plenary which was also attended by Djokanovic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall attending the meeting. I know that among those present were deputies and SDS members, but it is quite possible that there was several meetings running in parallel before the Assembly. However, I did attend this particular meeting where this concern was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that our strategic objectives took account of the Lisbon Agreement and our agreement with the Croats at Graz.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the accused please repeat the number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please repeat the number, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, can you tell us, the paper "Novi Vjesnik," who does it belong to and where was it published?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Novi Vjesnik" is a Croatian newspaper. I don't know where exactly it was published, probably in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could the next page be exposed on the other part of the screen because it's English version. Yeah. Next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Boban says down there: The agreement as recommended by the European community. Does this accord with your knowledge, indicating that this did not amount to any violation of the conference?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in my testimony here that when the conference ended, and I think it was held in Brussels, it was at the proposal of Mr. Cutileiro. Since the conference was not fruitful, he said that you can try and resolve certain problems bilaterally, and thus help find a solution to this problem. The Muslims did not want any part in this. We embarked on these negotiations bilaterally with the Croats, and on our way back from the conference stopped at Graz. And I think it was helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the penultimate page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What you said about the recommendation of the European community, that's where it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be admitted ?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's D4060, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we briefly have 1D9504, just to have it identified because the English version of the agreement has been admitted under this previous number. So let's put up the Serbian version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document? Is it the same document from Graz?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same document. I think that it was even archived in my case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it please be admitted either under a new number or along with the previous one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Previous one being the news clipping? We'll admit this separately.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D4061, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During the cross-examination, the Prosecution focused on the document called paper A and paper B to quite a degree. And then Mr. Vjestica, an MP and a high official was quoted as saying at an Assembly session that an operations plan should be adopted. Could you tell us why Vjestica would be asking for an operational plan if paper A and paper B were an official and binding plan?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That precisely says that, Vjestica, in a municipality where the Serbs were a minority, where they were threatened, there were, say, 10.000 Serbs on one side of the Una river, they were worried, he was worried, and he asked for an operations plan for defending this threatened Serb population. So documents A and B, I repeat once again, that document did not have any importance in the implementation of any decision of ours. I never felt that at least. Perhaps someone just mentioned that in passing, but in practice I never felt any significance of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Speaker, your Trial Chamber in the first-instance judgement, how did they treat paper A and paper B and the six strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think precisely as I have interpreted it just now. It did not attach any importance to the six strategic objectives or to documents A and B, as I read it. You can read it too and see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 24274, could it please be shown and then page 354. Paragraph 995 of the judgement. Page 354. I don't know which page it is in Serbian for paragraph 995. [In English] "It would be incorrect to place these goals on a pedestal, as the Prosecution does, for in the final analysis they are anodyne statements, serving as official state policy and even qualifying for publication in the Bosnian Serb Republic's Official Gazette ..." And few lines later: "An anachronistic reading of the May goals is not only inadvisable, it misses the point, just as an anachronistic reading of the December Instructions misses the point. The instructions and the goals lacked substance and utility ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it really helpful -- I mean, to the extent we are going to engage in this exercise, is it really helpful to point out the section and then skip over the very sentence which says that insidious hidden meanings can be found in the context and the events that follow. I mean, what kind of colloquy will result from that omission?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually Mr. Tieger didn't read that right. It says: "If one is inclined to find ... insidious" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's leave it. We have the document in front of us. What is the question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Speaker, this position taken in the final judgement, was it actually dismissed by the Appeals Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My assertion is no, but you can see easily from the appeals judgement that there is no qualification to the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked, Mr. Speaker, it was suggested that you were interested in military matters, that you talked to generals. Whose generals were they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what was shown in my case and what was explained in the judgement, I was interested in commanders at local level, municipal level, or even lower level, from the Army of Republika Srpska and the police. I wanted to express my interest in what was going on in the area where my parents lived, where my neighbours and friends lived, after all where my own house was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was -- were you a member of the Supreme Command and what kind of a body was that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the Supreme Command. It was an advisory body to the Presidency, or rather, the president of the republic as the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P3419 [as interpreted], could that please be displayed. 3149. Page 7 in Serbian. Then it must be number 8 in Serbian. That's not it. 05542154 is the ERN number of that page. The English is fine but not the Serbian, so could we have page 7. The typewritten page in Serbian, please. I don't know what these papers are. They're not part of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm seeing a different document in my e-court. Oh, it should be Exhibit 3149. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you said 3419. Yes, P3149.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Line 19, I said 3149.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yeah, that's first -- then eighth page in Serbian from this cover page. And please, some in English -- that is 9 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Speaker, I'm going to read what you said, it's at the bottom of the page. "Mr. Krajisnik: I was never more useless than here. I have not been consulted as a member of the Supreme Command about a single promotion or about a single decoration or about a single action, nor do I know and you have not submitted reports except to President Karadzic, so we are in the same ..." How does this correspond to your experience in terms of your work in the Supreme Command and your influence over military developments?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These words confirm what I said throughout my testimony. This is consistent with the role that I had in the Supreme Command and my position vis-à-vis military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what the attitude was of the military commands towards the influence of civilian authorities over command and control of the army?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most adequate word in the Serbian language would be "pristili se," that means that they strongly resisted any kind of influence at local levels and further up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From that point of view, what was the position of the ministers of defence?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were marginalised and they did not have any kind of influence. That was one of the reasons why Mr. Subotic resigned and that can be seen from his testimony in my trial and I believe that happened here, too, if he made a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dispute that, Mr. Speaker, did we have any knowledge and, according to that knowledge, did our army commit crimes? What was the attitude of our commanders towards crimes, rapes, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say from Mladic onwards, including all the other officers I knew, but I shall focus on Mladic. When General Mladic came into contact with us, anyway with me specifically, I always heard him being strongly opposed to the commission of any crime, especially as far as paramilitaries are concerned, that is to say, formations that were not under control. He always said criminals can never establish a state. I have to say that for the sake of the truth. For a while we did have this rift between us and Mr. Mladic, but I have to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I have no further questions -- well, I do have questions, but I haven't got the time needed for that. Thank you, once again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. Can I just show one more document, 65 ter 1368? Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wanted to make clear, the Chamber never has restricted your time to examine the witness. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. However, I'm making an effort to bring in as many witnesses as possible, so it's because of that, Excellency. It's not an objection addressed to you, no. I'm afraid that this is not the document. 65 ter 13468.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Mr. Speaker, did you have this record in your own trial, this record of the meeting of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few days ago during proofing, I saw this document for the first time or at least I do not remember having seen it. I would have remembered this observation had I seen this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please focus on this, the 28th of March, 1995. General Mladic is asking the minister not to interfere with promotions, and he's asking me to annul the minister's decision. How does this fit into what you said a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This fully reflects the relationship between the minister of defence and Mr. Mladic. Mr. Mladic, as a matter of fact, even received oral consent. The minister transferred the few powers he did have to him. He didn't want the minister to interfere in any way, to have any kind of influence over the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done. Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, for having come to testify on this holiday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you are tendering this document, the final one --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D4062, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Two quick matters arise for re-direct, Mr. President, very brief. I'm pretty confident they can be finished in five minutes, if not less. But if you want to break, that's fine too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the circumstances we'll continue -- but on what issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The first issue is a matter that was raised -- it concerns the June 10th meeting of -- it was raised yesterday, the June 10th meeting of the Presidency and the government. Mr. Krajisnik said -- addressed that in cross-examination and addressed it in a different manner which -- he addressed it in a way so that I didn't go to the -- to his testimony, and then addressed it in a different way in his re-direct examination. So I just want to present the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, at pages 43925 through 26 yesterday during your cross-examination, it was put to you that the meeting of the government preceded the meeting of the Presidency on June 10th, and then Mr. Djeric was tasked by the Presidency to submit a report on prisoners. And you said at line 9: "Yes, that's it." And then when Mr. Karadzic addressed the issue with you at 43936 you said: "And then in the afternoon the government looked at these problems on its own perhaps." So I wanted to confirm what you said in your own case in 2006, which is P -- found at 65 ter 25522 at page 25754. I know those are a lot of numbers. So I'll repeat the page --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that this has stemmed from the re-direct. I really don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll say it again. The witness said that he -- that the government was tasked by the Presidency. Then in re-direct he resiled from that and said: Well, it looks like the government did it on its own. So I want to go back to what he said in 2006. It's very directly arising from the re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the Chamber allowed the re-cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the page number was 25754. If you can actually start at 25753 on the very bottom so we can see where we are. "These are the minutes from the 25th government session held the same day date, chaired by Mr. Djeric ..." and then we move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then the question at line 11: "Now, Mr. Krajisnik, that was Mr. Djeric's immediate response to the assignment he had received at the session of the Presidency the same day; correct?" Then you started saying, well: [As read] "It could be the other way around, that what he said could -- I don't know which session ... it could be, you're really right -- you're really right, this consultative meeting could have been in the morning and this session ... yes, you are right. He was given that task and he entrusted it to the Ministry of Justice."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I just want to tender that page so there's no misunderstanding about that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're not asking any question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, that is, in fact, an accurate reflection of what you said in 2006 when that issue was presented to you in your own trial; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I don't understand the question, but I'll try to interpret it. There were two --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, hold on --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- sessions --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- I'm asking you -- I'm asking you if that is an accurate reflection of what you said -- what you testified to in your own case in 2006. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember these very words. I can tell you today what I exactly think and then it's up to you to decide. I don't remember what I said in 2006. I can explain to you today how it was and what I know about it. I don't know what happened in 2006. Maybe there's a mistake in the transcript. I can tell you now what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You testified to it on direct -- on cross, you testified to it on re-direct. I am putting this document to you. If you don't remember it, then I want to tender the document for impeachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow the witness to continue. Yes, please continue, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, both then and now I remember that on the same day, the 10th of June, there were two meetings. One was an extended meeting of all the leaders which was called at the time the National Security Council or whatever. Mr. Djeric was there, the prime minister. In the meeting of that meeting [as interpreted] which I saw subsequently, there's a question of prisoners raised and the need to investigate that, what the conditions were, et cetera. Later on I know that the government met, and I interpreted what was stated there. What Mr. Djeric was given, what he was briefed about autonomously in that meeting without our presence, he entrusted the minister to investigate the matter and that is the entire statement that I can make. I don't know any other details. I attended the first meeting, whereas I wasn't present at the government meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why shouldn't we take a look at P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, just a second. It's not for you at this time to interfere. Are you done, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With that. And I just had one more contextual matter to raise, which is a matter of 30 seconds, I think. Yes, I -- so I tender that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- to be added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll add those two pages to the exhibit. In the meantime, have the parties sorted out the -- with respect to the interview? Is it safe if we add only those two pages, pages 27 and 28?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, although we would ask that the entire interview be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, we'll add those two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The only contextual issue I wanted to raise then, Mr. President, was with regard to 65 ter 30861, the intercepted conversation between Mandic and David or David. At lines -- at page 19 through 20 of this transcript, the accused asked Mr. Krajisnik: "It states those of our lot wanting to cleanse or mop-up Dobrinja, however, Karadzic would not allow them to go ahead ..." There is an ellipsis in the intercept itself, and it goes on, the speaker goes on to say: "There is no need any longer." So in case the document doesn't ultimately get into evidence, I wanted the context to be clearer on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Robinson, do you have any observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I do. I don't understand how Mr. Tieger can make a speech without the -- asking a question to the witness as part of the re-examination. That means he asks a question to the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we upload that part, MFI D4058. Mr. Krajisnik, is it next page in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it might still be page 3 -- it's page 3 in the English. It's presumably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's -- I think the English page is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, English page is correct. I think we're still on the cover page for the -- the first page for the B/C/S, so it needs that -- it needs to be moved. And one more page. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you see that portion of the intercept where Mr. Mandic refers to "ociste," and that's the portion that Mr. Karadzic asked you the insistence on "'ociste' Dobrinja, however, Karadzic does not let them." And is it correct he continues with Mandic saying before he concludes what he's saying: "He doesn't want any more ... there is no need any longer"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Fourth line in Serbian for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I need to see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mean the previous page?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, the next one should refer to what you're asking me about. Just a moment, please. I can't see where it says what Mandic said. Perhaps you can direct me with the assistance of the interpreters. I can't find it. Oh, it seems that it must be the previous page. I'm sorry, my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I think the first portion begins on the previous page and then it continues on to this page, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says "there's no need any longer," this is completely out of context. I don't know what he was referring to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just turn to --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because David says --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll turn to the previous page. Let me direct you, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Could we go to the previous page, page 3 in B/C/S, the bottom. "Ovi su nasi ..." you see that? That's the part that Dr. Karadzic directed your attention to? And then continue on to the next page?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So that's what he showed you: "Our guys insisted to 'ociste,'" and then it continue -- Mandic continues: "He doesn't want any more ... there is no need any longer." I just wanted to confirm that that's what the -- what was stated in the intercept at the portion that Mr. Karadzic directed your attention to.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it means. All I can do is to confirm that it's written here, "there's no need any longer," but I really cannot understand what he wanted to say, Mandic. I mean, he says it's the end of Alija and what -- what does it have to do with Dobrinja. I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that confirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: One clarification for this, Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: About this intercept? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take a look at towards the bottom where Mandic says: "There is a shorter route. They opened the road. Fine. They're doing it and working and I think that it will soon pass through Dobrinja ..." Does this help you to understand that -- what was said later: "There was no need for that any longer"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question for me? Well, I could understand that in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "There is a shortcut" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we can see it. Well, unless my colleagues have a question for you, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Krajisnik. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it again. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank you once again with my review for proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll rise all together. Given the circumstances, we'll adjourn for the week. But I take it you will continue to do your utmost not to -- or to spend the time as efficiently as possible. And we'll resume on Tuesday next week. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 26th day of November, 2013, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.46 a.m.,
